title: The tiger's milk
hookLine: a queen's strange illness, a cure no one could fetch, and a boy who rides home on a tigress
carry: kshama: forgiveness is a mark of the divine
tomorrow: on the path up Ayyappa's hill, why is every stranger called swami?

cards: The prescription is impossible on purpose. The queen of Pandalam lies in a darkened room, clutching her head. The palace physician bows and gives his verdict: only one cure will work, the milk of a tigress.
The room goes silent. Nobody walks into the forest and milks a tiger, and the physician knows it. Because the illness, in the story, isn't real.
It's a plan to send someone into the forest who isn't supposed to come back. Today, the boy who went anyway.

teach.b: In the telling, after the king adopts Manikandan, the queen has a son of her own. A scheming minister whispers to her that the adopted boy will take the throne from her child.
Afraid, she agrees to pretend to be ill, and the physician is in on it. Manikandan is still young. He hears what the cure is, and he offers to go.
The king begs him not to.
The boy goes anyway, alone, into the forest, with a bundle of food for the road. He simply goes to fetch what his mother says she needs.
In the forest, tradition says, he meets the demoness Mahishi and overcomes her, which was why he was born.
Then he comes home, not with a pot of milk, but riding on a tigress, with tigers walking behind him. The queen and the minister, seeing him, understand what they've done, and fall at his feet.
And here the story puts its weight. Not on punishment, but on forgiveness.
Manikandan forgives them, and tells the king who he is and why he came.
Hindu teachers rank forgiveness high: in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna lists kshama, forgiveness, among the divine qualities, the marks of a person turned toward God.
The god of the forest hill answers a trap with care, and the people who set it with pardon. Notice who he forgives: not a stranger, but family, the one who should have kept him safe.
That's the hardest kind, and the story says that's where the divine shows most.

how: Ayyappa is often shown seated on or beside a tiger, and devotees retell how Manikandan went into the forest for tiger's milk and came home riding a tigress.

games.q: what does “kerala's onam and ayyappa” mean?
o: a festival king, and a boy sent away for stealing milk
a festival king, and a boy who rode home on a tigress
a festival king, and a boy who fought his own brother

games.q: the tiger's milk — tap the pairs.

s: the Bhagavad Gita counts forgiveness among the divine qualities
Krishna lists kshama, forgiveness, among the qualities of a person turned toward God (Gita 16).
in the story, the queen's illness was a pretense
afraid for her own son's place, she pretended, and the physician was in on it.
the story ends with the plotters punished
it ends with the queen and the minister asking forgiveness, and Manikandan forgiving them.

games.q: you're Manikandan, home on a tigress. the queen and the minister who sent you to die fall at your feet. what do you do?
o: forgive them, and tell the king who you are and why you came.
let the tigers chase them out of the palace.
leave without a word and never come back.
games.why: he forgives them: kshama, forgiveness, which the Gita counts among the divine qualities.

practice: Bring to mind someone who once set you up, or wished you less than well. Don't force forgiveness, and forgiving never means staying where you're still being hurt.
Just hold their face a breath longer than you want to, the way Manikandan stood before the queen, breathing in steadiness and breathing out the grudge.
If you pray, say Ayyappa's pilgrims' chant softly with each breath: Swamiye saranam Ayyappa.

wordCard.voice: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa. Today, the tiger's milk: a cure meant as a trap, a boy who went anyway, his return on a tigress, and his pardon. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a tigress, the animal Ayyappa is told to have ridden home to the palace.

carryVoice: Your line: kshama, forgiveness is a mark of the divine. The boy came home on a tigress, and forgave. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: the Ayyappa story: the queen's feigned illness, the tiger's milk, the defeat of Mahishi, the return on a tigress
sources.work: Ayyappa tradition of Kerala (Pandalam and Sabarimala retellings)
